title: Post-intubation hypotension
trigger: New hypotension after RSI, tube placement, or positive-pressure ventilation.
immediateMoves: Confirm pulse, blood pressure, waveform, oxygenation, and tube depth.
Disconnect briefly if severe auto-PEEP/dynamic hyperinflation is plausible.
Reduce excessive PEEP or tidal volume while maintaining oxygenation.
Give IV fluid bolus 500-1000 mL crystalloid if preload-dependent physiology is suspected.
Push-dose epinephrine 5-20 mcg IV every 2-5 minutes: mix 1 mL of 0.1 mg/mL (cardiac) epinephrine into 9 mL saline = 10 mcg/mL; give 0.5-2 mL per dose.
Start norepinephrine early at 0.05-0.1 mcg/kg/min and titrate to MAP.
Consider tension pneumothorax, mainstem intubation, hemorrhage, sepsis, or peri-intubation arrest physiology.
reassess: ETCO2 waveform
Lung sliding/bilateral breath sounds
Vent pressures
Repeat BP every 1–2 minutes until stable
avoid: Do not assume the tube is the only problem.
Do not forget analgesia/sedation after paralysis wears off.
references: Heffner AC, et al. Incidence and factors associated with cardiac arrest complicating emergency airway management. Resuscitation. 2013;84(11):1500-1504. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.resuscitation.2013.07.022
Russotto V, et al. Intubation Practices and Adverse Peri-intubation Events in Critically Ill Patients (INTUBE). JAMA. 2021;325(12):1164-1172. https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2021.1727
Society of Critical Care Medicine. Guidelines for the Management of Critically Ill Adults with Airway Management. Crit Care Med. 2023. https://doi.org/10.1097/CCM.0000000000005819
Verify local institutional policy and the equipment stocked where you work.

title: Failed airway / cannot intubate
trigger: Failed attempts, falling oxygen saturation, poor view, inability to ventilate, or airway contamination.
immediateMoves: Call failed-airway plan out loud and assign roles.
Reoxygenate with two-hand BVM, oral/nasal airway, PEEP valve, and suction.
Change something before the next attempt: operator, blade, position, device, bougie, or approach.
Place supraglottic airway if BVM or intubation is failing and time allows.
Move to front-of-neck access if cannot oxygenate.
reassess: SpO2 trend
Chest rise
ETCO2 if ventilating
Number of attempts
Time since paralysis
avoid: Do not repeat the same failed attempt.
Do not burn the last 30 seconds debating while oxygenation is failing.
references: Difficult Airway Society. Guidelines for the management of unanticipated difficult intubation in adults. 2025. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bja.2025.02.001
Difficult Airway Society. DAS airway algorithms. https://das.uk.com/guidelines/das_intubation_guidelines
Verify local institutional policy and the equipment stocked where you work.

title: Arterial puncture during central line
trigger: Bright pulsatile blood, arterial waveform, high-pressure tubing, or ultrasound concern during access.
immediateMoves: Stop. Keep wire/catheter controlled; do not dilate if position is uncertain.
Confirm with ultrasound, pressure transduction, blood gas, or waveform if stable enough.
If only small finder/needle puncture, remove and hold firm pressure.
If dilator or large catheter entered artery, leave it in place and call vascular/surgery immediately.
Document event, site, exam, and consultation.
reassess: Distal pulses
Expanding hematoma
Airway compression risk for neck sites
Neurovascular status
avoid: Never pull a large-bore arterial catheter and 'just hold pressure' without the right backup.
references: Bowdle A. Vascular complications of central venous catheter placement: evidence-based methods for prevention and treatment. J Cardiothorac Vasc Anesth. 2014;28(2):358-368. https://doi.org/10.1053/j.jvca.2013.02.027
Guilbert MC, et al. Arterial trauma during central venous catheter insertion: case series, review and proposed algorithm. J Vasc Surg. 2008;48(4):918-925. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jvs.2008.04.046
Verify local institutional policy and the equipment stocked where you work.

title: Lost guidewire / wire control problem
trigger: Wire no longer visible or control of the proximal wire is lost.
immediateMoves: Stop the procedure immediately.
Do not advance catheter or dilator blindly.
Obtain imaging to localize the wire if not immediately retrievable.
Call IR/vascular based on local resources.
File safety event and document honestly.
reassess: Patient rhythm
Chest symptoms
Wire location
Need for retrieval
avoid: Do not pretend it did not happen.
references: Vannucci A, et al. Retained guidewires after intraoperative placement of central venous catheters. Anesth Analg. 2013;117(1):102-108. https://doi.org/10.1213/ANE.0b013e3182599179

The Joint Commission. Sentinel Event Alert: preventing unintended retained foreign objects. https://www.jointcommission.org/resources/sentinel-event/sentinel-event-alert-newsletters/sentinel-event-alert-issue-51-preventing-unintended-retained-foreign-objects/
Verify local institutional policy and the equipment stocked where you work.

title: Failed transvenous pacer capture
trigger: Pacer spikes without electrical/mechanical capture, persistent bradycardia, or unstable hypotension.
immediateMoves: Confirm generator is on, rate appropriate, output high, and connections secure.
Increase mA until capture, then set safety margin above threshold.
Slowly advance/withdraw catheter while watching ECG and patient pulse/BP.
Use ultrasound/fluoro/CXR if available to confirm course.

Continue transcutaneous pacing while troubleshooting; if hypotensive, start push-dose epinephrine 5-20 mcg IV every 2-5 minutes (1 mL of 0.1 mg/mL cardiac epinephrine into 9 mL saline = 10 mcg/mL, give 0.5-2 mL per dose) or norepinephrine infusion 0.05-0.1 mcg/kg/min titrated to MAP.
reassess: Electrical capture
Mechanical pulse
Blood pressure
Pain/sedation needs
Catheter depth
avoid: Do not accept electrical spikes as success without a pulse/BP response.
references: Glikson M, et al. 2021 ESC Guidelines on cardiac pacing and cardiac resynchronization therapy. Eur Heart J. 2021;42(35):3427-3520. https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehab364
American Heart Association. Part 9: Adult Advanced Life Support, 2025 CPR and ECC Guidelines. https://cpr.heart.org/en/resuscitation-science/cpr-and-ecc-guidelines/adult-advanced-life-support
Verify local institutional policy and the equipment stocked where you work.

title: Procedural sedation apnea
trigger: Hypoventilation, apnea, desaturation, loss of airway tone, or rising ETCO2 during sedation.
immediateMoves: Stop sedative dosing and call for airway help.
Reposition airway, jaw thrust, suction, and add oral/nasal airway as needed.
BVM with PEEP if ventilation inadequate.

Reversal only when appropriate for agent/context and never instead of ventilation: opioid - naloxone 0.04-0.4 mg IV, titrate every 2-3 minutes; benzodiazepine - flumazenil 0.2 mg IV over 15 seconds ONLY in benzodiazepine-naive patients (seizure risk).
Prepare for intubation if oxygenation or ventilation cannot be maintained.
reassess: ETCO2 waveform
Chest rise
SpO2
Hemodynamics
Return of protective airway reflexes
avoid: Do not stare at the pulse ox while the patient is not ventilating.
references: American Society of Anesthesiologists. Practice Guidelines for Moderate Procedural Sedation and Analgesia. Anesthesiology. 2018;128(3):437-479. https://doi.org/10.1097/ALN.0000000000002043

American College of Emergency Physicians. Clinical Policy: Procedural Sedation and Analgesia in the Emergency Department. Ann Emerg Med. 2014;63(2):247-258. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.annemergmed.2013.10.015
Verify local institutional policy and the equipment stocked where you work.

title: Local anesthetic systemic toxicity (LAST)
trigger: Early warning - stop injecting and reassess: numbness or tingling of the lips, mouth or tongue (perioral), ringing in the ears or tinnitus, metallic taste, light-headedness, blurred or double vision, drowsiness, agitation or confusion.
Established toxicity: seizure, altered mental status, dysrhythmia, or cardiac arrest. May occur immediately or up to 60 minutes after injection.
The prodrome may be absent or unobservable under sedation or general anaesthesia, where a dysrhythmia or sudden hypotension can be the first sign. Absence of early symptoms does not exclude LAST.
immediateMoves: Stop local anesthetic injection immediately.
Call for 20% lipid emulsion (Intralipid) now — this is the antidote and must not be delayed.
Secure airway early if seizure or loss of consciousness: high-flow O2, prepare to intubate.
If cardiac arrest: start ACLS; avoid vasopressin; use standard epinephrine doses sparingly (≤1 mcg/kg); begin lipid emulsion simultaneously.
Lipid emulsion 20%: bolus 1.5 mL/kg IV over 1 minute, then infusion 0.25 mL/kg/min; may repeat bolus in refractory arrest (max cumulative dose ~12 mL/kg).
Treat seizure with benzodiazepine (midazolam 1-2 mg IV, or 0.05 mg/kg, repeat as needed); avoid propofol (myocardial depressant and dilute lipid — not a substitute for Intralipid).
reassess: Rhythm and BP every 1-2 minutes until stable
Mental status and seizure recurrence
Response to lipid emulsion — cardiac recovery is the therapeutic endpoint
SpO2 and ETCO2 continuously if intubated
avoid: Do not give vasopressin in LAST cardiac arrest (ASRA guideline).
Do not use propofol as a substitute for lipid emulsion — it causes myocardial depression.
Do not give high-dose epinephrine — small doses only (≤1 mcg/kg) if needed.
Do not assume resolution is complete — CNS toxicity may outlast cardiac toxicity; observe ≥4-6 hours.
references: Neal JM, et al. The Third American Society of Regional Anesthesia and Pain Medicine Practice Advisory on Local Anesthetic Systemic Toxicity. Reg Anesth Pain Med. 2018;43(2):113-123. https://doi.org/10.1097/AAP.0000000000000720

Di Gregorio G, et al. Clinical presentation of local anesthetic systemic toxicity: a review of published cases, 1979 to 2009. Reg Anesth Pain Med. 2010;35(2):181-187. https://doi.org/10.1097/AAP.0b013e3181d2310b

ASRA Pain Medicine. Checklist for Treatment of Local Anesthetic Systemic Toxicity. 2020. https://www.asra.com/guidelines-articles/original-articles/article-item/asra-news/2020/11/01/checklist-for-treatment-of-local-anesthetic-systemic-toxicity
Verify local institutional policy and the equipment stocked where you work.

title: Pneumothorax after central venous catheter
trigger: Respiratory distress, hypoxia, or decreased breath sounds following IJ, subclavian, or axillary central venous catheter placement.
immediateMoves: Assess immediately: vital signs, O2 saturation, breath sounds bilaterally, JVD, tracheal position.
Bedside ultrasound: absent lung sliding ipsilateral to line site confirms pneumothorax.
For tension physiology (hypotension + absent breath sounds + JVD or tracheal deviation): needle decompression immediately — do not wait for imaging.
For large or symptomatic pneumothorax without tension: chest tube or pigtail catheter.
For small, asymptomatic pneumothorax: supplemental O2, serial imaging, close monitoring in a monitored setting.
reassess: Vital signs and SpO2 every 15 minutes
Lung sliding on repeat ultrasound
Repeat CXR at 4-6 hours for observed small pneumothorax
Response to chest tube drainage (air leak on water seal, lung re-expansion)
avoid: Do not dismiss absent lung sliding ipsilateral to a subclavian or IJ line as artifact.
Do not delay needle decompression for tension pneumothorax to obtain imaging.
Do not attempt a contralateral central line without first securing the ipsilateral pneumothorax.
Do not clamp a chest tube in a suspected ongoing air leak without expert guidance.
references: Hind D, et al. Ultrasonic locating devices for central venous cannulation: meta-analysis. BMJ. 2003;327(7411):361. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmj.327.7411.361
Roberts ME, et al. British Thoracic Society Guideline for pleural disease. Thorax. 2023;78(Suppl 3):s1-s42. https://doi.org/10.1136/thorax-2022-219784
Verify local institutional policy and the equipment stocked where you work.

title: Chest tube malposition
trigger: Poor drainage, persistent air leak, respiratory deterioration, pain out of proportion, or imaging showing tube in fissure, subcutaneous tissue, or abdomen after chest tube or pigtail catheter placement.
immediateMoves: Obtain CXR immediately: confirm tube position, presence of residual pneumothorax or effusion, and diaphragm relationship.
Confirm the drainage circuit is not kinked, clamped, or obstructed before declaring malposition.
Subcutaneous tube (no drainage, crepitus tracking along tube): remove and replace — provides no pleural drainage.
Intrafissural tube (tube in the major or minor fissure): may drain slowly; replace or add a second tube if drainage is inadequate.
Tube traversing the diaphragm into the abdomen: stop drainage immediately; do not pull without surgical consultation — intra-abdominal hemorrhage risk.
reassess: Drainage output and character every 1-2 hours after repositioning
Air leak assessment: fluctuation in water seal chamber with respiration
Repeat CXR after repositioning or replacement
Hemodynamics and oxygenation
avoid: Do not advance a chest tube after initial placement — introduces a non-sterile segment into the pleural space.
Do not clamp the tube for a suspected large bronchopleural fistula without expert guidance — tension pneumothorax risk.
Do not remove a tube that has crossed the diaphragm without surgical presence and a vascular injury plan.
Do not assume inadequate drainage is tube failure before ruling out circuit obstruction.
references: Bosman A, et al. Malpositions of thoracic drains: a retrospective analysis. Eur J Cardiothorac Surg. 2010. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22349999/
Roberts ME, et al. British Thoracic Society Guideline for pleural disease. Thorax. 2023;78(Suppl 3):s1-s42. https://doi.org/10.1136/thorax-2022-219784
Verify local institutional policy and the equipment stocked where you work.

title: Laryngospasm
trigger: Sudden partial or complete glottic closure during or after sedation, airway manipulation, or extubation. Presents as stridor (partial) or silent obstruction with paradoxical chest movement and desaturation (complete).
immediateMoves: Remove all airway stimuli immediately: stop suctioning, airway manipulation, and the precipitating procedure.
100% O2 via tight-fitting BVM mask; jaw thrust and chin lift to optimize airway alignment.
Apply CPAP-level pressure with the BVM (10-20 cmH2O) — sustained positive pressure may break partial laryngospasm.
If not breaking within 30-60 seconds: succinylcholine 0.1-0.2 mg/kg IV (subparalyzing dose) to break spasm; prepare for possible intubation.
If complete obstruction and impending arrest: succinylcholine 1-2 mg/kg IV and immediate intubation. Have surgical airway ready.
reassess: SpO2 and ETCO2 continuously
Chest rise with each positive-pressure breath — absence indicates complete closure
Resolution of stridor (partial → resolved)
HR: bradycardia during severe laryngospasm signals impending cardiac arrest
avoid: Do not force a laryngoscope or airway device through a closed glottis — worsens spasm and laryngeal trauma.
Do not use jaw thrust without BVM mask seal — Larson's point maneuver (bilateral firm pressure at the condylar notch posterior to the jaw ramus) may help break spasm without an airway device.
Do not delay succinylcholine if BVM ventilation is failing.
Do not use ketamine for sedation without suction immediately available — increased secretions can precipitate laryngospasm.
references: Gavel G, Walker RWM. Laryngospasm in anaesthesia. Contin Educ Anaesth Crit Care Pain. 2014;14(2):47-51. https://doi.org/10.1093/bjaceaccp/mkt031
Larson CP. Laryngospasm - the best treatment. Anesthesiology. 1998;89(5):1293-1294. https://doi.org/10.1097/00000542-199811000-00056
Verify local institutional policy and the equipment stocked where you work.

title: Air embolism during central or large-bore access
trigger: Sudden hypoxia, hypotension, chest pain, altered consciousness, or cardiovascular collapse around an open hub - during insertion, while a line is disconnected, or at removal.
immediateMoves: Occlude the hub or the open lumen immediately; clamp, cap, or cover the site.
Left lateral decubitus, head down, to trap air at the right ventricular apex and away from the outflow tract.
100% oxygen to speed nitrogen washout from the bubble.
Aspirate from a central lumen if one is already in place and the tip is central.
Support the circulation: IV fluid bolus, and norepinephrine 0.05-0.1 mcg/kg/min titrated to MAP or push-dose epinephrine 5-20 mcg IV every 2-5 minutes.
Start CPR if arrested - chest compressions can also break up a large air lock.
Call for help and consider hyperbaric referral for suspected cerebral arterial gas embolism.
reassess: SpO2 and end-tidal CO2 (a sudden fall in ETCO2 fits a large embolism)
Blood pressure and rhythm
Neurological status, including focal deficit suggesting arterial gas embolism
Whether every hub and lumen is now closed
avoid: Do not leave a large-bore sheath or catheter hub open to air at any point, including during removal.
Do not sit the patient up.
Do not delay occluding the hub in order to obtain imaging.
references: Mirski MA, et al. Diagnosis and treatment of vascular air embolism. Anesthesiology. 2007;106(1):164-177. https://doi.org/10.1097/00000542-200701000-00026
McCarthy CJ, et al. Air embolism: practical tips for prevention and treatment. J Clin Med. 2016;5(11):93. https://doi.org/10.3390/jcm5110093
Verify local institutional policy and the equipment stocked where you work.

title: Re-expansion pulmonary oedema after pleural drainage
trigger: Repetitive cough, chest tightness or pain, or worsening breathlessness during or shortly after pleural drainage - usually after a large or rapid volume, but it can follow a small one.
immediateMoves: Stop draining and clamp the drain. Slowing it is not enough.
Sit the patient up and give high-flow oxygen; titrate to saturation.
Do not resume drainage in this session. If more must come off later, drain slowly and stop at the first symptom.
Escalate respiratory support early: CPAP or non-invasive ventilation for hypoxia that does not correct, and intubation with lung-protective settings if it progresses.
Support the circulation with fluids and, if needed, norepinephrine 0.05-0.1 mcg/kg/min titrated to MAP. This is a permeability oedema, so diuretics are not the treatment and may worsen hypovolaemia.
Chest x-ray to confirm unilateral oedema on the drained side and exclude pneumothorax as the cause of deterioration.
reassess: SpO2 and work of breathing every 5 minutes until stable
Whether the drain is clamped and stays clamped
Blood pressure - hypotension is common and is not a reason to diurese
Chest x-ray for unilateral oedema on the drained side
Total volume already removed this session
avoid: Do not keep draining to 'finish the job' once symptoms start.
Do not give diuretics reflexively - this is not volume overload.
Do not attribute new hypoxia after drainage to the effusion itself without excluding pneumothorax.
Do not use vacuum bottles or wall suction for therapeutic aspiration; suction increases this risk.
references: Roberts ME, et al. British Thoracic Society Guideline for pleural disease. Thorax. 2023;78(Suppl 3):s1-s42. https://doi.org/10.1136/thorax-2022-219784
Sohara Y. Reexpansion pulmonary edema. Ann Thorac Cardiovasc Surg. 2008;14(4):205-209. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18818568/
Verify local institutional policy and the equipment stocked where you work.

title: Orbit still tense after canthotomy
trigger: The lateral canthotomy is made but the orbit has not decompressed: the globe is still tense and proptotic, the intraocular pressure is still raised, and vision or the pupil has not improved.
The lower lid does not swing freely away from the globe when pulled outward and downward - the release is incomplete.
immediateMoves: Treat this as an incomplete cantholysis until proven otherwise. The skin incision is only the approach; releasing the inferior crus of the lateral canthal tendon is the treatment.
Clear the field before cutting again: gentle pressure and gauze. Bleeding hides remaining tendon.
Grasp the lower lid with toothed forceps and pull it outward and downward to put the inferior crus on tension, then strum for the taut band running to the lateral orbital rim.

Cut the remaining inferior crus with blunt-tipped scissors directed toward the orbital rim, inferiorly and slightly posteriorly, away from the globe. The lid should then swing freely and the globe should soften.
Reassess after the release: orbital tension, intraocular pressure, proptosis, and vision or at least light perception with the pupil.

Release the superior crus only when all three are still true after a genuinely complete inferior release - the orbit is still tense, the pressure is still raised, and vision or the pupil has not improved. It adds lacrimal artery and gland risk.
Call ophthalmology emergently and continue medical measures to lower intraocular pressure under their guidance, but do not wait for either to finish the release.
reassess: Whether the lower lid swings freely away from the globe
Globe tension and proptosis on gentle palpation
Intraocular pressure if a tonometer is available
Vision or light perception and the pupil, after each release
Time from symptom onset to decompression
avoid: Do not accept the skin incision as the procedure. Without the cantholysis the orbital pressure is unchanged.
Do not move to the superior crus to compensate for an incomplete inferior release - an incompletely released inferior crus is far commoner than a genuine need to go superior.
Do not cut toward the globe, and do not substitute sharp or iris scissors for blunt-tipped ones in a swollen, bloody field.
Do not keep manipulating the orbit if globe rupture is suspected - stop and get emergent ophthalmology.
references: Rowh AD, et al. Lateral canthotomy and cantholysis: emergency management of orbital compartment syndrome. J Emerg Med. 2015;48(3):325-330. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jemermed.2014.11.002
U.S. Joint Trauma System. Eye Trauma: Initial Care Clinical Practice Guideline. 2021. https://jts.health.mil/assets/docs/cpgs/Eye_Trauma_Initial_Care_01_Jun_2021_ID03.pdf
American Academy of Ophthalmology EyeWiki. Orbital Compartment Syndrome. https://eyewiki.aao.org/Orbital_Compartment_Syndrome
Verify local institutional policy, the ophthalmology consultation pathway, and which blunt scissors are stocked on the eye tray.

title: Needle position uncertain during pericardiocentesis
trigger: Blood back in the syringe, or blood that clots briskly, and no proof of where the tip is - about to dilate, pass a wire, or railroad a catheter.
Bright pulsatile return, new ventricular ectopy as the needle advances, or a tip that cannot be seen in the fluid pocket on ultrasound.
immediateMoves: Stop. Do not dilate and do not railroad a catheter until position is proven.
The colour of the aspirate answers nothing - in haemopericardium everything is blood.

Prove position with agitated saline: inject a few millilitres and watch where the bubbles appear. Bubbles in the pericardial space confirm position; bubbles in the right ventricle mean the tip is inside the heart.

Alternatives when saline contrast is unavailable or equivocal: see the needle, wire, or catheter itself in the pericardial space on real-time ultrasound, or transduce the hub - a ventricular pressure waveform means the tip is in the ventricle.
Brisk clotting in the syringe supports intracardiac blood, since pericardial blood is usually defibrinated and does not clot. Treat it as a supporting sign, never as the confirmation.
If intracardiac: withdraw the needle, watch, and re-scan for a new or enlarging effusion. A needle hole usually seals.

Then re-plan rather than repeat: pick the largest pocket with the shortest safe path, read the depth off the screen, and advance under real-time visualisation. Activate cardiothoracic surgery and blood if the effusion enlarges or the patient deteriorates.
reassess: Where the bubbles went on agitated saline
Whether the wire, and then the catheter, is seen inside the pericardial space before anything is dilated
Rhythm and blood pressure - new ectopy suggests the tip is against or in myocardium
Repeat ultrasound for a new or enlarging effusion after any withdrawal
Residual effusion and whether tamponade physiology has actually resolved
avoid: Do not use the colour of the aspirate as confirmation.
Do not dilate or railroad a catheter over a wire that has not been seen inside the pericardial space.
Do not treat withdrawal of an intracardiac needle as the end of it - re-scan for a new or enlarging effusion.
Do not repeat blind passes at the window that just found the heart.
Do not read failure to improve after drainage as proof the needle was misplaced - clot, a second loculated pocket, or a different obstructive shock can all do that.
references: Ainsworth CD, Salehian O. Echo-guided pericardiocentesis: let the bubbles show the way. Circulation. 2011;123(4):e210-e211. https://doi.org/10.1161/CIRCULATIONAHA.110.005512

Tsang TS, et al. Consecutive 1127 therapeutic echocardiographically guided pericardiocenteses: clinical profile, practice patterns, and outcomes spanning 21 years. Mayo Clin Proc. 2002;77(5):429-436. https://doi.org/10.4065/77.5.429
European Society of Cardiology. 2025 ESC Guidelines for the management of myocarditis and pericarditis. Eur Heart J. 2025;46(40):3952-4041. https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehaf192
Verify local institutional policy, the pericardiocentesis set stocked in your department, and the surgical escalation pathway.

title: No return of circulation after thoracotomy
trigger: The chest is open and there is still no organised cardiac activity, no pulse, and no measurable pressure after the incision, the pericardiotomy, or the aortic cross-clamp.
immediateMoves: Work the recoverable technical failures in order before reaching for the endpoint.
Exposure first. The commonest technical failure is a small incision: extend it from the sternal edge to the table, and across the sternum to a clamshell for right-sided injury or wider access.
Confirm the pericardium is genuinely open. A tamponaded pericardium is tense and hard to pinch up - grasp and incise it longitudinally, anterior to the phrenic nerve, and evacuate clot.

Hunt the cardiac wound: inspect the posterior surface and the great vessels, lifting the heart carefully. Control with finger pressure first, then a Foley balloon, staples, or sutures, and do not tie a suture around a coronary artery.

Two-handed internal cardiac massage throughout, with blood products running. Internal defibrillation only for a shockable rhythm and at the low energy internal paddles use - commonly of the order of 10-20 J, confirmed against the paddle and defibrillator instructions rather than assumed.
If the clamp is on and nothing changed, question the clamp before the patient. It is probably on the oesophagus - check by feel against the orogastric tube - or the bleeding is above it.
Expect brisk bleeding from the divided internal mammary arteries the moment circulation returns in a clamshell. Look at the sternal edges first and ligate them.
reassess: Organised cardiac activity and a perfusing rhythm - the resuscitation endpoint
Whether the incision truly runs from the sternum to the table
Whether the pericardium is open and decompressed, or only incised over a tense sac
Aortic clamp position under direct vision and by feel against the orogastric tube, with the clamp time said out loud every five minutes
Sternal edges for internal mammary bleeding once circulation returns
Blood product delivery and whether the theatre and surgeon are still a real destination
avoid: Do not keep massaging through an inadequate incision. Extend it.
Do not accept 'pericardium opened' without evacuated clot and a decompressed sac.
Do not leave a clamp that has not been identified under direct vision and by feel against the orogastric tube.
Do not carry on past the endpoint: no organised cardiac activity after tamponade release, haemorrhage control, and an aortic clamp. Stop there.
references: Burlew CC, et al. Western Trauma Association critical decisions in trauma: resuscitative thoracotomy. J Trauma Acute Care Surg. 2012;73(6):1359-1363. https://doi.org/10.1097/TA.0b013e318270d2df

Seamon MJ, et al. An evidence-based approach to patient selection for emergency department thoracotomy: a practice management guideline from the Eastern Association for the Surgery of Trauma. J Trauma Acute Care Surg. 2015;79(1):159-173. https://doi.org/10.1097/TA.0000000000000648
Western Trauma Association. Adult Emergency Resuscitative Thoracotomy Algorithm and Procedure Guide. 2024. https://westerntrauma.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/02/ERT-Algorithm-Procedures.pdf
Verify the institutional trauma algorithm that governs signs of life, CPR windows, and termination, and confirm the tray holds a sternal-division instrument and compatible internal paddles.
